question: How does Content Security Policy (CSP) protect against XSS?

options.text: CSP blocks all JavaScript on the page
options.explanation: CSP doesn't block all JS. It allows scripts from a whitelist (script-src 'self' cdn.com). Only scripts from unauthorized sources and inline scripts are blocked

options.text: CSP encrypts scripts before executing them in the browser
options.explanation: CSP doesn't encrypt anything. It tells the browser: 'execute scripts only from these domains'. If XSS injects a <script> tag, it's blocked because inline scripts are forbidden

options.text: CSP removes dangerous HTML tags from the server response
options.explanation: CSP doesn't modify HTML. It's a header directive for the browser. HTML sanitization is the server's job (DOMPurify, xss). CSP is the last line of defense

options.text: CSP controls where the browser can load scripts from -- inline scripts and scripts from unauthorized domains are blocked

question: Why are SameSite cookies the best CSRF protection for modern APIs?

options.text: SameSite encrypts the cookie so the attacker can't read it
options.explanation: SameSite doesn't encrypt (that's what the Secure flag + HTTPS do). SameSite controls WHEN the cookie is sent -- not with cross-origin requests

options.text: SameSite: strict/lax prevents the browser from sending cookies with cross-origin requests -- evil.com won't get bank.com's cookie
SameSite automatically generates a CSRF token
options.explanation: SameSite doesn't generate tokens. It replaces the need for CSRF tokens by simply not sending cookies on cross-origin requests

options.text: SameSite makes the cookie invisible to JavaScript
options.explanation: That's what the httpOnly flag does, not SameSite. SameSite controls cookie sending in cross-origin requests. httpOnly protects against XSS (document.cookie)

question: What is NoSQL injection and how do you protect against it?

options.text: Injecting JavaScript into MongoDB through eval
options.explanation: While $where and eval are dangerous, typical NoSQL injection is passing operators ($gt, $ne, $exists) through unvalidated input. express-mongo-sanitize solves this problem

options.text: SQL injection in MongoDB -- protection is the same as for SQL databases
options.explanation: MongoDB doesn't use SQL. NoSQL injection is passing MongoDB operators through JSON. { email: { $gt: '' } } will return the first user instead of a specific one

options.text: Passing MongoDB operators ($gt, $ne) through input -- protection: express-mongo-sanitize (removes $ and .) + Zod validation
NoSQL injection is impossible because MongoDB doesn't use SQL
options.explanation: Not using SQL doesn't mean it's safe. MongoDB operators ($gt, $ne, $regex) allow bypassing filters. { password: { $ne: '' } } will bypass password verification

question: Why is the regular expression /^(a+)+$/ dangerous (ReDoS)?

options.text: Only in Node.js -- other languages are not vulnerable to ReDoS
options.explanation: ReDoS affects all languages with a backtracking regex engine: JavaScript, Python, Java, Ruby, .NET. Only RE2 (Go, Rust) uses a linear algorithm

options.text: Regex consumes a lot of RAM when processing long strings
options.explanation: ReDoS is a CPU problem, not RAM. The regex engine tries an exponential number of paths, overloading the CPU. This enables a DoS attack through a single HTTP string

options.text: Nested quantifiers (a+)+ create an exponential number of backtracking paths on strings like 'aaaaab'
It's an infinite loop -- the regex will never complete
options.explanation: It's not an infinite loop -- the regex will complete, but on a 25-character string it can take minutes/hours. The number of backtracks grows exponentially: 2^n

question: Which headers does Helmet set by default?

options.text: X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff -- disables MIME-sniffing
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN -- clickjacking protection
Strict-Transport-Security -- forces HTTPS
Authorization: Bearer -- automatic JWT authentication
options.explanation: Helmet doesn't manage authentication. Authorization is a request header from the client, not a server response header. Helmet sets security headers in responses
